L42: Pentagon official Emil Michael on Thursday said that Anthropic is still considered a "cite12†supply chain risk ," a day after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the company is "back on the right side."
L43: Why it matters: The cite13†Trump administration is not entirely aligned on one of the world's leading AI labs following months of cite14†fighting over how the military can use its models.
L44: 
L45: What they're saying: "Anthropic is still a designated Supply Chain Risk at @DeptofWar and for the Defense Industrial Base. Thank you for your attention to this matter!" Michael cite15†posted on X†x.com .
L46: Catch up quick: Lutnick cite16†told Axios' Mike Allen on the sidelines of the cite17†G20 Innovation Summit this week: "We trust Anthropic."
L47:   * "They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side. So the answer is: Yes," Lutnick said when asked if he trusts Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
L48:   * Personality cite18†differences under Amodei's leadership added fuel to the fire in a clash between the Trump administration and Anthropic earlier this year, but the company has been elevating co-founder cite19†Tom Brown 's role in its relationship with the White House.
L49: Yes, but: A federal judge in August cite20†struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a cite12†supply-chain risk , but the company is still fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit.
L50: 
L51: The bottom line: Anthropic is not completely out of the woods with the Trump administration as Brown increasingly takes center stage.

L34: Multiple new cases have been filed against OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT played a role in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.

L37: cite25†Image: OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman listens to a question from U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick at the G20 Innovation Ministerial summit, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, U.S., September 2, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Drake The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman (pictured above) of aiding and abetting a mass shooting, as well as negligence [Jonathan Drake/Reuters]
L38: 
L39: By cite26†Al Jazeera Staff L40: 
L41: 2 Sep 2026
L42: OpenAI is facing another wave of lawsuits in the wake of the February mass shooting in cite27†Tumbler Ridge in Canada’s province of British Columbia, which left eight people dead.
L43: 
L44: On Wednesday, 30 new complaints were reportedly filed in a United States federal court in California, including teachers and students who were witnesses and survivors at the school where most of the shooting took place, joining seven initial lawsuits filed in April.
L45: ## Recommended Stories
L46: 
L47:   * cite28†AI used to create viruses not found in nature for first time L48:   * cite29†US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law L49:   * cite30†John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years L50:   * cite31†OpenAI says it detected malign activity months before Hugging Face attack L51: 
L52: The lawsuits accuse the San Francisco, California-based artificial intelligence giant and its CEO, Sam Altman, of negligence, as well as aiding and abetting a mass shooting.
L53: The suits, brought by lawyer Jay Edelson, allege that the company knew about the intentions of the 18-year-old shooter who, in her interactions with OpenAI’s chatbot ChatGPT, had described scenarios involving gun violence, but that the leadership did not report their concerns to law enforcement, echoing earlier lawsuits on the matter.
L54: 
L55: In April, Altman penned a letter to the community apologising that the company did not alert law enforcement about the shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar.
L56: “While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote in the letter.
L57: 
L58: Authorities say that cite32†Van Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother before going to the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and opening fire. Five children and one educator were killed at the school. More than 25 others were wounded before Van Rootselaar died from what police described as a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
L59: One of the new cases filed was on behalf of a 13-year-old identified as A C, who played dead after watching the shooter kill their classmates and the teacher. Another new case was brought by a grade seven teacher named Deidre Rushlow, who hid under her desk with her students during the rampage.
L60: “There isn’t a day that goes by that I don’t think about what happened at Tumbler Ridge, or the victims of this devastating tragedy and their families. It’s a constant and sobering reminder of the important and incredibly difficult work that many people in my team do each and every day,” Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s head of strategy, cite33†wrote†x.com in a post on X on Wednesday.
L61: “We’ve been approaching this litigation with respect for both the legal process and the families and victims of this tragedy, and we’ll continue to engage in good faith with that process.”
L62: 
L63: Edelson did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
L64: ## Growing legal pressure
L65: 
L66: In July, British Columbia’s Attorney General Niki Sharma cite34†announced that the province would also pursue “all legal avenues to hold OpenAI and its decision-makers accountable” for the shooting.
L67: 
L68: The company has faced a growing slate of suits, apart from the ones from British Columbia, alleging that its product played a role in incidents that led to users harming others and themselves.
L69: A recent lawsuit in Florida alleges that the company “actively assisted and encouraged the mass shooting” at Florida State University in April 2025.
L70: 
L71: There are other complaints filed on behalf of victims across the US and Canada alleging that the victims took their own lives after being pushed by ChatGPT to do so, including cite35†a case in Quebec earlier this year.

L145@P6: MANY WORLDS’ TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATIONS
L146@P6: 25. At the time of the Many Worlds Asserted Patents’ inventions, recommendation
L147@P6: engines were largely limited to observing a user’s past behavior and then attempting to predict
L148@P6: what the user may like in the future based on the user’s past choices. Further, a feature that prior
L149@P6: recommendation engines lacked was the ability to explain why a user received a recommendation.
L150@P6: This gap deprived the user of valuable information that may give context to a specific
L151@P6: recommendation from a recommendation engine and thus improve the user experience.
L152@P6: 26. Prior to the Many Worlds Asserted Patents, recommendation engines
L153@P6: predominantly used collaborative filtering: analyzing which users consumed which content,
L154@P6: grouping users with similar consumption patterns, and recommending to each user what similar
L155@P6: users consumed. This approach had critical technical limitations that degraded recommendation
L156@P6: quality. First, pure collaborative filtering is content-agnostic. It treats all content items as opaque
L157@P6: identifiers without analyzing what the content actually contains. The system might know that users
L158@P6: who liked item #47 also liked item #93, but it has no understanding whether these are short stories
L159@P6: or long novels, jazz or rock music, or comedy or drama podcasts. Second, this content-blind
L160@P6: approach creates cold-start problems: new content with few user interactions cannot be effectively
L161@P6: recommended even if its attributes would appeal to many users. Third, the black-box nature
L162@P6: provides no transparency, as users receive recommendations with no explanation of why the
L163@P6: system believes they will enjoy the content, reducing trust and engagement. These were not merely
L164@P6: business problems but specific technical deficiencies in how computer systems processed and
L165@P6: utilized recommendation data.

L167@P6: objects, topic objects, and links between the objects.

L0@P0: BILLING CODE 7020-02
L1@P0: INTERNATIONAL TRADE COMMISSION
L2@P0: [Investigation No. 337-TA-1448]
L3@P0: Certain Video-Capable Laptop, Desktop Computers, Handheld Computers,
L4@P0: Tablets, Televisions, Projectors, and Components and Modules Thereof; Notice
L5@P0: of a Commission Determination Not to Review an Initial Determination
L6@P0: Granting a Joint Motion to Terminate the Investigation in Its Entirety;
L7@P0: Termination of the Investigation
L8@P0: AGENCY: U.S. International Trade Commission.
L9@P0: ACTION: Notice.
L10@P0: SUMMARY: Notice is hereby given that the U.S. International Trade Commission
L11@P0: has determined not to review an initial determination (“ID”) (Order No. 48) of the
L12@P0: presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”) granting a joint motion to terminate the
L13@P0: investigation in its entirety based on arbitration agreements. The investigation is
L14@P0: terminated.
L15@P0: FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Lisa A. Murray, Esq., Office of
L16@P0: the General Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street, S.W.,
L17@P0: Washington, D.C. 20436, telephone (202) 205-2781. Copies of non-confidential
L18@P0: documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the
L19@P0: Commission’s electronic docket (EDIS) at https://edis.usitc.gov. For help accessing
L20@P0: EDIS, please email EDIS3Help@usitc.gov. General information concerning the
L21@P0: Commission may also be obtained by accessing its Internet server at
L22@P0: https://www.usitc.gov. Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this
L23@P0: matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission’s TDD terminal, telephone
L24@P0: (202) 205-1810.
L25@P0: This document is scheduled to be published in the
L26@P0: Federal Register on 2026-09-03 and available online at
L27@P0: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-18026, and on
L28@P0-1: https://govinfo.govSUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The Commission instituted this
L29@P1: investigation on May 19, 2025, based on a complaint filed by Nokia Technologies Oy
L30@P1: and Nokia Corporation, both of Espoo, Finland (collectively, “Nokia”). 90 FR
L31@P1: 21335-36 (May 19, 2025). The complaint, as supplemented, alleges violations of
L32@P1: section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1337, based on the
L33@P1: importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the
L34@P1: United States after importation of certain video-capable laptop, desktop computers,
L35@P1: handheld computers, tablets, televisions, projectors, and components and modules
L36@P1: thereof by reason of the infringement of certain claims of U.S. Patent No. 10,536,714
L37@P1: (“the ’714 patent”); 8,050,321 (“the ’321 patent”); 9,036,701 (“the ’701 patent”); and
L38@P1: 11,805,267 (“the ’267 patent”). Id. The complaint further alleges that a domestic
L39@P1: industry exists. Id.
L40@P1: The notice of investigation names the following respondents: Hisense Co.,
L41@P1: Ltd. of Qingdao, China; Hisense USA Corporation of Suwanee, Georgia; Hisense
L42@P1: Electronics Manufacturing Company of America Corporation of Suwanee, Georgia
L43@P1: (collectively, “Hisense”); Acer America Corporation of San Jose, California, and
L44@P1: Acer Inc. of Xizhi, Taiwan (collectively, “Acer”); and ASUSTeK Computer Inc. of
L45@P1: Taipei City, Taiwan, and ASUS Computer International of Fremont, California
L46@P1: (collectively “ASUS”). Id. The Office of Unfair Import Investigations (“OUII”) is
L47@P1: also named as a party. Id.
L48@P1: On September 25, 2025, the Commission terminated the investigation as to
L49@P1: claims 4, 8, 11, 14, 18, 22, 25, 28, and 29 of the ’714 patent; claims 4, 7, 11, 14, 15,
L50@P1-2: 17, 18, and 20 of the ’701 patent; claim 11 of the ’321 patent; and claims 4, 6, 10, 12-18, 22, 24, 28, and 30-36 of the ’267 patent. Order No. 17 (Sept. 5, 2025),
L51@P2: unreviewed by Comm’n Notice (Sept. 25, 2025).
L52@P2: On November 20, 2025, the Commission terminated the investigation as to
L53@P2: claims 5, 7, 12, 19, 21, and 26 of the ’714 patent, and claims 3 and 10 of the ’701
L54@P2: patent. Order No. 22 (Sept. 22, 2025), unreviewed by Comm’n Notice (Nov. 20,
L55@P2: 2025).
L56@P2: On February 20, 2026, the Commission terminated the investigation as to
L57@P2: claim 9 of the ’321 patent and claim 30 of the ’714 patent. Order No. 34 at 2, Order No.
L58@P2: 35 at 2, both unreviewed by Comm’n Notice (Feb. 20, 2026).
L59@P2: On April 2, 2026, the Commission terminated the investigation as to Hisense
L60@P2: based on settlement. Order No. 39 (Mar. 18, 2026), unreviewed by Comm’n Notice
L61@P2: (Apr. 2, 2026).
L62@P2: On July 17, 2026, Nokia, Acer, and ASUS filed a joint motion to terminate the
L63@P2: investigation in its entirety based on arbitration agreements. The motion included as
L64@P2: exhibits both the confidential and public versions of the arbitration agreements
L65@P2: between Nokia and Acer and between Nokia and ASUS. The motion states that there
L66@P2: are no other agreements, written or oral, express or implied, between the private
L67@P2: parties concerning the subject matter of the investigation, and that it is in the interest
L68@P2: of the public and administrative economy to grant the motion. On July 29, 2026,
L69@P2: OUII filed a response supporting the joint motion to terminate.
L70@P2: On July 30, 2026, the ALJ issued the subject ID (Order No. 48) pursuant to
L71@P2: Commission Rule 210.21(d), 19 CFR 210.21(d), granting the joint motion to
L72@P2-3: terminate based upon arbitration agreements. The ID finds that the joint motion complies with Commission Rule 210.21(d), and that granting the motion “will
L73@P3: conserve public and private resources.” ID at 4.
L74@P3: No petitions for review of the ID were filed.
L75@P3: The Commission has determined not to review the ID. The investigation is
L76@P3: terminated in its entirety.
L77@P3: The Commission vote for this determination took place on August 31, 2026.
L78@P3: The authority for the Commission’s determination is contained in section 337
L79@P3: of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1337), and in Part 210 of the
L80@P3: Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure (19 CFR Part 210).
L81@P3: By order of the Commission.
